title: SCOTUSblog Founder Tom Goldstein Sentenced to Six Years for Tax Evasion
excerpt: The once-prominent Supreme Court litigator was convicted on 12 felony counts tied to millions in hidden poker winnings, offshore accounts, and mortgage fraud.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Lydia Kay Griggsby sentenced Thomas Goldstein, 56, to six years in federal prison on Friday for tax evasion and mortgage fraud tied to his secret life as a high-stakes poker player.
  • A jury convicted Goldstein in February on 12 of 16 charges, including hiding millions in poker winnings from the IRS and lying on mortgage applications.
  • Prosecutors had sought over eight years and $3.1 million in restitution; Goldstein's defense argued for supervised release, citing a gambling addiction.
  • Goldstein plans to appeal with former U.S. Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar on his legal team.

Thomas Goldstein, the once-celebrated Washington attorney who argued more than 40 cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and co-founded the widely read legal news site SCOTUSblog, was sentenced Friday to six years in federal prison for tax evasion and mortgage fraud stemming from his secret career as a globe-trotting high-stakes poker player.

U.S. District Judge Lydia Kay Griggsby handed down the sentence at a hearing in Greenbelt, Maryland, calling Goldstein's conduct "serious and concerning, not only in terms of the nature of it but its breadth." She also acknowledged his contributions to the legal profession, saying SCOTUSblog was "groundbreaking and has really reshaped our legal community and how we talk about the law."

At the end of the hearing, Griggsby revoked Goldstein's bond and ordered him taken into custody.

From the Supreme Court Bar to the Poker Table

Goldstein, 56, built an improbable career at the pinnacle of American law. Unlike many elite appellate lawyers who relied on Ivy League degrees and prestigious clerkships, he broke into the exclusive ranks of the Supreme Court bar through an entrepreneurial approach, according to the Wall Street Journal. His client roster included Alphabet's Google, "Fortnite" maker Epic Games, and he was part of the team that represented Al Gore in the landmark Bush v. Gore case that decided the 2000 presidential election.

https://x.com/DOJFraudDiv/status/2080769433761415608

But as his star rose in legal circles, so did his appetite for poker. What began as casual games around the office escalated into international matches with millions of dollars on the line. Prosecutors alleged he raked in roughly $50 million in poker winnings in 2016 alone, though Goldstein estimated he ultimately lost about $10 million through the peaks and valleys of his gambling.

A Scheme Built on Offshore Accounts and False Returns

During the six-week trial, prosecutors laid out what they called a textbook tax evasion scheme. Goldstein funneled poker winnings through offshore bank accounts, concealed nearly $5 million from the IRS, shaved millions off his true law firm income, and directed people to pay his creditors directly to avoid showing the transactions on his books, according to the Department of Justice.

He also lied on mortgage applications in 2021 when seeking financing for a $2.6 million Washington, D.C., home, omitting more than $14 million in liabilities including two promissory notes and unpaid IRS obligations, which enabled him to secure a $1.98 million loan.

A federal jury convicted Goldstein in February on 12 of the 16 charges he faced: one count of tax evasion, four counts of willful failure to timely pay taxes, four counts of aiding in the preparation of false tax returns, and three counts of making false statements to mortgage lenders.

"His motivation was singular: pure, unrelenting greed."

— Federal prosecutors, in a court filing

The Trial That Featured a Spider-Man Star

The case drew national attention partly because of its unusual cast of characters. Actor Tobey Maguire, who starred in the 2002 film "Spider-Man," testified during the trial that he had hired Goldstein in 2020 to recover more than $7 million that a Texas businessman allegedly owed the actor from a poker debt, according to Reuters.

Goldstein himself took the stand, citing a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him as the catalyst for his intensified gambling. "You only live once," he told jurors, describing how the health scare drove him deeper into a world where players risked fortunes on informal agreements.

A Courtroom Plea for Leniency

Goldstein grew emotional as he addressed the judge before sentencing. "There is no question that I have deeply disappointed people, that I have not held myself to the standards that I should be held to as somebody who's a lawyer and a prominent lawyer, that I have caused people real pain," he said, according to the Wall Street Journal.

His defense attorneys had urged Griggsby to impose a lengthy supervision period rather than prison time, arguing that Goldstein suffered from a "severe and longstanding gambling addiction" that unraveled his judgment. They noted that his legal practice largely involved advocating for plaintiffs' lawyers, state and local governments, and people with limited access to Supreme Court practitioners.

Prosecutors pushed for more than eight years and $3.1 million in restitution for unpaid taxes, describing his crimes as "coldly calculated" and his attempts to conceal them as "brazen." They pointed to a lifestyle "replete with Bentleys, globe-trotting vacations, and a $200,000 watch."

What Comes Next

Goldstein was charged in January 2025 during the final days of the Biden administration. He has maintained his innocence and plans to appeal to the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He recently added former U.S. Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar of law firm Cooley to his defense team, signaling his preparation for the appellate fight.

Post-trial court filings also raised questions about whether Goldstein continued gambling while on pretrial release. His 2025 tax return reported over $1.7 million in gambling income, according to Bloomberg Tax, though his attorneys said he had been "fully compliant" with release conditions.

The case is United States v. Thomas Goldstein, U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, No. 8:25-cr-00006-LKG.
nri_angle: The case highlights the scrutiny facing high-profile professionals in the U.S. legal system, resonating with Indian-American attorneys and finance professionals navigating complex tax obligations.
